strengths: UniAP addresses an important practical problem: choosing pipeline partitions together with layer-specific DP, TP, and FSDP strategies. This integration has clear potential usefulness for training large vision models with limited memory and communication bandwidth.

Table 1 demonstrates meaningful throughput improvements. On ENVB-8, ViT-Huge achieves 45.58 samples/s versus 38.74 for Alpa and 32.20 for Galvatron; Swin-Huge improves from 13.90 to 19.08 samples/s over Galvatron. The reported 3.80× Llama-7B improvement is also substantial.

The evaluation covers five model families and four hardware environments, including non-NVIDIA accelerators. Table 4 provides useful evidence of near-linear weak scaling to 64 DCUs. Matching baseline throughput while substantially reducing strategy-search time is itself valuable.

The workflow and strategy visualizations are understandable, particularly the BERT case study in Appendix G. Hardware, model, and solver configurations aid reproducibility, and Appendix F reports a encouraging 3.59% mean throughput-estimation error on the selected ENVA/ENVB strategies.
weaknesses: The stated optimization has a material correctness gap. Equations (6a–c) enforce stage contiguity but do not enforce increasing stage indices along graph edges. For a two-layer chain u→v, assigning u to stage 2 and v to stage 1 satisfies the placement and contiguity constraints. Equation (4) then charges zero communication for this edge because it counts only transfers from stage j to j+1. Thus the formulation admits artificially cheap assignments; Appendix B proves contiguity without resolving this issue.

The core solver formulation is incomplete. Equations (3) and (4) contain fourth-degree products such as P_ui P_vi S_uk S_vl, so they are not quadratic as written. Auxiliary-variable reformulations can address this, but the necessary variables and linking constraints are not supplied. This is a potentially repairable specification gap that nevertheless prevents unambiguous reproduction of the central Gurobi optimization.

The repeated optimality claims exceed the evidence. Appendix E specifies a 60-second limit and early termination after 15 seconds when the optimality gap is below 4%, without reporting achieved gaps or termination statuses. Section 3.5 consequently bounds a procedure with capped solver time, not the time required to certify an optimum. Even certified solutions would concern the restricted candidate space and approximate cost model. Together with the feasible-set problem, these gaps outweigh the demonstrated engineering gains and determine my Weak Reject recommendation.

GPipe memory feasibility is insufficiently specified. Algorithm 1 passes micro-batch size b to CostModeling, Section 3.2 scales activation memory by the supplied batch size, and Equation (5) includes no explicit dependence on the number of micro-batches c. GPipe retains activations across micro-batches before backward execution, so the description does not establish that this accumulation is accounted for. Reported throughput-estimation accuracy does not validate peak-memory estimates.

The evidence does not isolate joint optimization as the source of improvement over hierarchical methods. Figure 6 compares against inter-layer-only and intra-layer-only variants, rather than a hierarchical variant sharing the same candidates and cost model. Hierarchical optimization is not inherently suboptimal. Differences in cost-model accuracy and multithreaded versus single-threaded search also affect the comparisons. Moreover, strategy-search timing measures UOP and excludes profiling, leaving total planning overhead unquantified.
